content: The potential benefits of chlorine-based methods in rinse water persistence were explored in various studies. Casanova et al. (2018) conducted a simulation study on personal protective equipment (PPE) doffing practices in a medical biocontainment unit. Ten healthcare workers (HWs) experienced in Ebola virus disease (EVD) care donned and doffed PPE following unit protocols, which included guidance from trained observers and the use of alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR). A mixture of Φ6 (enveloped virus), MS2 (non-enveloped virus), and a fluorescent marker was applied to four PPE sites to simulate body fluid viral load. After performing a patient care task, the HWs doffed their PPE, and samples were taken from inner gloves, face, hands, scrubs, and environmental sites with visible fluorescent markers. The study found that MS2 transfer was highest on inner gloves (7 out of 10 participants), with lower contamination observed on scrubs (2 participants) and hands (1 participant). Most participants (8 out of 10) had only one positive contamination site. Environmental samples with visible fluorescent markers were negative for viral contamination. The study highlighted that repeated contact of gloves with PPE during doffing could lead to inner glove contamination, even with ABHR use between doffing steps. Human factors, such as mishandling PPE, significantly contributed to contamination risks. To minimize viral load on inner gloves, careful doffing and stronger glove-sanitizing agents (e.g., hypochlorite or povidone-iodine) may be necessary, especially for non-enveloped viruses, which are more resistant to ABHR. Casanova et al. (2016) conducted another simulation study with 15 HWs donning EVD PPE. Virus was applied to PPE, and participants were guided through the doffing protocol by a trained monitor. Ten participants used ABHR for glove and hand hygiene, while five used hypochlorite for glove hygiene and ABHR for hand hygiene. After doffing, MS2 virus was detected on the dominant inner glove of 8 participants, the non-dominant inner glove of 6 participants, and scrubs of 2 participants. All MS2 contamination on inner gloves occurred when ABHR was used for glove hygiene, while no contamination was observed with hypochlorite use. The study emphasized the importance of careful doffing to minimize hand contamination and recommended stronger sanitizing agents like hypochlorite for glove hygiene. Lantagne et al. (2018) conducted a multi-thread research study to provide evidence for disinfection guidelines. Their findings included the following: 1. The chemistry of chlorine sources impacts the shelf life of chlorine solutions (ranging from less than 1 day to 30 days). Testing chlorine solutions is recommended to ensure accuracy. A 0.5% chlorine solution with a 15-minute exposure time effectively reduces transmission risk. 2. Community handwashing with chlorine solutions is as safe and effective as handwashing with soap and water or sanitizer. Chlorine solutions offer the added benefit of reducing pathogen persistence in rinse water. 3. High-test hypochlorite (HTH) performed particularly well, with the longest shelf life, minimal hand irritation, and the highest handwashing efficacy. However, HTH poses operational challenges, such as being more explosive than sodium dichloroisocyanurate (NaDCC) and forming precipitates that can clog pipes. Proper training and maintenance can mitigate these issues. Reidy et al. (2017) reviewed PPE solutions for UK military medical personnel in an Ebola treatment unit (ETU) in Sierra Leone. They emphasized the importance of tactility and dexterity through the use of two pairs of gloves, selecting 400-mm nitrile, powder-free gloves. A nine-day pre-deployment training program allowed over 60 clinical personnel per deployment to practice PPE skills in simulated ETUs and classrooms. The training provided evidence-based PPE solutions, skills in donning and doffing PPE, confidence in selected PPE, and testing of individual capabilities. Gao et al. (2016) evaluated the effects of ABHR applications on the integrity of 13 brands of nitrile and latex medical exam gloves. They found that tensile strength decreased with each ABHR application, with nitrile gloves being more affected than latex gloves. Ethanol-based ABHR caused less change in tensile strength compared to isopropanol-based ABHR. The investigators recommended that hospital staff practice using ABHR and doffing gloves to become familiar with changes in glove properties. The systematic review did not identify evidence on PPE breaches or exposures, compliance, human factors, or health worker confidence. However, it highlighted the importance of structured doffing protocols, effective hand hygiene agents, and the need for comprehensive infection prevention and control measures to protect healthcare workers and patients.
